paragraphs.heading: A satellite for cosmology
paragraphs.text: The Cosmic Background Explorer, or COBE (said KOH-bee), was a NASA satellite devoted to cosmology. Also known as Explorer 66, it worked from 1989 to 1993. Its task was to study the cosmic microwave background, or CMB, and gather measurements that would shape how we understand the cosmos. It was the second CMB satellite, after RELIKT-1. Two more advanced craft came after it: WMAP, which ran from 2001 to 2010, and Planck, which ran from 2009 to 2013.

paragraphs.heading: What it found
paragraphs.text: COBE delivered two key pieces of evidence for the Big Bang theory. The CMB has an almost perfect black-body spectrum, and it has very faint anisotropies, meaning small differences in brightness between one patch of sky and another. John C. Mather of NASA Goddard Space Flight Center and George F. Smoot III of the University of California, Berkeley shared the 2006 Nobel Prize in Physics for discovering the blackbody form and anisotropy of the CMB. The Nobel committee described COBE as the point where cosmology began to be a precision science.

paragraphs.heading: What it measured
paragraphs.text: The mission set out to measure the spread-out radiation between 1 micrometre and 1 cm in wavelength, over the whole sky. It recorded three things. First, the spectrum of the 3 K radiation from 100 micrometres to 1 cm. Second, how that radiation varied across the sky at 3 to 10 mm. Third, the spectrum and sky pattern of the diffuse infrared background from 1 to 300 micrometres.

paragraphs.heading: A slow road to launch
paragraphs.text: NASA approved the plan on the condition that it cost less than US$30 million, leaving out the launcher and data analysis. Overruns in the Explorer program caused by IRAS, the Infrared Astronomical Satellite, meant building only began at Goddard Space Flight Center in 1981. To save money, COBE's infrared detectors and liquid helium dewar were made much like those on IRAS. COBE was meant to ride a Space Shuttle in 1988, but the Challenger explosion grounded the Shuttles. A redesigned COBE finally went up on a Delta rocket on 18 November 1989, into a Sun-synchronous orbit.

paragraphs.heading: Built for precision
paragraphs.text: Every source of error had to be controlled and measured, which called for a careful, integrated design. The satellite turned slowly, at 0.8 rpm, to keep errors in its anisotropy readings in check. Its circular Sun-synchronous orbit, 900 km up with a 99° inclination, gave full sky coverage, kept out stray radiation and held the instruments at a steady temperature. The orbit tracked the line between day and night on Earth all year. Together with the spin axis, the orbit kept the Earth and Sun below the shield, so COBE could scan the full sky every six months.

paragraphs.heading: Keeping cold
paragraphs.text: A 650 L superfluid helium cryostat, called a dewar, kept the FIRAS and DIRBE instruments cold for the length of the mission. A cone-shaped shield blocked direct radiation from the Sun and Earth, along with radio noise from Earth and from COBE's own transmitting antenna. Layers of insulating blanket on the shield kept the dewar thermally isolated. In January 1994 engineering work ended, and the craft was handed over to Wallops Flight Facility to serve as a test satellite.

paragraphs.heading: Spotting the ripples
paragraphs.text: One instrument, the Differential Microwave Radiometer (DMR), mapped the sky at 31.4, 53 and 90 GHz using three radiometers, which are microwave receivers. Each one switched quickly between a pair of horn antennas, measuring the difference in brightness between two points in the sky 60° apart. For large-scale anisotropies, it was sensitive to about 3E-5 K.
